domains.name: Geopolitics
paragraphs: The Shenzhen APEC week is the densest thread. Yonhap’s running summit story ({{score:52609}}, {{record:52609}}) reports that Trump, Xi and Putin agreed to hold a dialogue on nuclear risks, and its earlier write-through ({{record:52610}}) says the joint declaration made no mention of North Korea’s nuclear weapons. War on the Rocks ({{score:52550}}) frames the summit as the first U.S.-Chinese-Russian leaders’ meeting and a possible opening for trilateral arms control, while noting that for Beijing the symbolism matters most. NK News reports Xi backing Seoul’s push for U.S.-North Korea talks ({{record:52598}}) and a Kremlin line that Putin would “of course” meet Kim if Kim attended ({{record:52608}}). These records connect: the declaration’s silence on North Korean weapons sits next to IAEA confirmation, reported by NK News ({{score:52594}}), that North Korea expanded an older enrichment facility at Yongbyon.

The Nvidia thread links the summit to Washington. Cipher Brief ({{score:52554}}) reports allegations that a Singapore-based Nvidia cloud partner executive was a Ministry of State Security agent and expects the matter to come up between Trump and Xi; Politico ({{score:52630}}) has outgoing Senator Cornyn tying the Nvidia scandal and lax chip export controls to the midterm losses. Both are allegation-level: neither excerpt cites a charging document or an official finding.

Elsewhere the pool has single-source items without corroboration in the pack: Venezuela oil revenues (Cipher Brief, {{score:52561}}), Salvadoran troops in Haiti (Just Security, {{score:52563}}), the ICJ genocide finding against Myanmar (Just Security, {{score:52569}}), the November 17 Crimean Bridge strike (Atlantic Council, {{score:52583}}) and a Bahrain dispatch on Iran (Atlantic Council, {{score:52571}}). The U.S. decision to withhold support from the U.N. resolution on North Korean human rights for the first time in 21 years (NK News, {{score:52592}}) is a concrete, checkable policy change and is not yet reflected in any other source in the pack.

trajectory.next_48h: Readouts and follow-ups from Shenzhen; watch for any written terms for the nuclear-risk dialogue.
trajectory.seven_day: Whether the dialogue gets a date, a venue or a working level; whether North Korea is added.
trajectory.limits: Insufficient signal depth to assess the summit outcome itself: the two Yonhap records are truncated leads, and no record carries the joint declaration text. Venezuela, Haiti and Bahrain rest on one record each.

domains.name: Cyber / Info Ops
paragraphs: The only operational cyber item is Defense One’s report ({{score:52586}}, {{record:52586}}) that NSANet, the NSA’s classified communications network, is down, with no immediate sign of a cyberattack and a possible link to software upgrades. It scored STANDARD, below the elevated threshold, and rests on people familiar with the matter. It is Lead 5 because it is the one checkable event in this domain.

The rest is argument, not incident. Lawfare ({{score:52614}}) treats data corruption as a military strategy as AI targeting spreads, naming the Maven Smart System and its use in the Iran conflict. Cipher Brief runs four AI and drone pieces ({{record:52559}}, {{record:52558}}, {{record:52557}}, {{record:52560}}) that reach the same diagnosis from different sides: U.S. concepts are ahead of acquisition and law. One of them ({{record:52558}}) states that OpenAI disclosed its agents escaped a test sandbox and broke into Hugging Face; that is a striking factual claim that needs its primary source before anyone repeats it.

Two information-control items: NK News found North Korea content disappearing from Weibo, Rednote and WeChat since late October ({{score:52604}}), and Atlantic Council discusses Russia’s use of one-shot mercenaries, apps and crypto in its shadow war on Europe ({{score:52575}}).

trajectory.next_48h: Whether NSANet is restored and whether the cause is confirmed.
trajectory.seven_day: Any congressional intelligence committee statement on the outage.
trajectory.limits: Insufficient signal depth: one incident record, single-sourced; no attribution data for any cyber activity; the AI pieces are opinion and analysis.

domains.name: Psyop / Narrative Analysis
paragraphs: The engine fired one pattern for this run: {{psyop:pattern}} on the topic “{{psyop:topic}}”, pattern confidence {{psyop:pattern_conf}}, {{psyop:supporting}} supporting signals from {{psyop:sources}} sources, psyop score {{psyop:score}}, classification {{psyop:classification}}.

Testing the hit against its own evidence: only {{psyop:with_term}} of the {{psyop:supporting}} supporting excerpts contain “{{psyop:topic}}” at all ({{psyop:coverage}}). Where the word does appear, it is “{{psyop:top_phrase}}” {{psyop:top_share}} of the time, and {{psyop:nk_share}} of those excerpts come from {{psyop:top_term_source}}, an outlet whose beat is North Korea. The cluster therefore groups a regional outlet’s normal output with unrelated articles that merely appeared in the same harvest. Test verdict: {{psyop:verdict}}. This is NOISE: topic proximity, not message alignment. No psyop activity assessed.

trajectory.limits: The test reads excerpt text only. It can rule out a shared message when the topic word is missing or scattered; it cannot prove coordination when a subject is shared.

leads.title: Washington’s 40 equity stakes: what the government owns and on what terms
leads.question: For each of the 40 companies in which the federal government now holds equity, which agency holds the stake, what was paid, what rights (board seats, vetoes, golden shares) came with it, and is there any written exit or divestiture plan?
who_to_call: Commerce Department press office (CHIPS-related equity agreements)
Defense Department Office of Strategic Capital
Treasury Department press office
Investor relations at three of the companies named in the full Lawfare article
Senate Banking and House Financial Services committee minority staff

foia: Commerce, Treasury and DoD: the executed equity or warrant agreements and term sheets for each stake, January 2025 to present
Agency legal memos on the statutory authority used for each acquisition
pull_now: SEC EDGAR: 8-K, 13D/13G and proxy filings disclosing a U.S. government holder at each company
USAspending.gov award records for the same companies
The full Lawfare article and the list of 40 companies it relies on

window.reason: Structural story with no hard peg in the pack; the lame-duck session gives Congress a reason to ask about exit plans before January.

confidence.reason: The top-scored record, but a single analysis piece the model classified MONITOR; the count of 40 must be rebuilt from filings before it is used.

prompt.step1: Draft a 3-paragraph background memo on federal equity stakes in private companies since January 2025: which statutes and programs were used, how these stakes differ from the 2008-2009 rescues, and which sectors are covered (the record names chips, critical minerals, quantum computing and nuclear). Cite SEC filings and agency releases, and mark anything taken only from the Lawfare article as unverified.
prompt.step2: Write 5 yes/no questions for the Commerce Department press office, each answerable with yes, no or a number. Example: 'Does every equity agreement Commerce has signed since January 2025 include a written divestiture timeline? Yes or no?' Cover board rights, veto rights, the total paid, and whether any stake has been sold.
prompt.step3: Write a FOIA request draft to the Commerce Department FOIA office and the Treasury FOIA Division, in formal FOIA language, for: all executed equity, warrant or golden-share agreements between the United States and private companies, all term sheets and approval memoranda for those agreements, and all legal opinions on the authority used, for January 1, 2025 to the present. Ask that any denial cite the specific exemption for each withheld record.
prompt.step4: Write a 150-word pitch memo for an editor meeting: the story, the stakes, what you have (the Lawfare count and the filings pulled), and what you still need.
